clue.text: Most sensational tablets stored in container for preacher

indicators.note: goods stored in a place sit inside it, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: the raised enclosed stand from which a sermon is delivered
E is slang for an ecstasy tablet, so tablets are Es

explanation.surface: A tabloid-style sermon: sensational pills found hidden in a pulpit.
explanation.walkthrough: The ecstasy tablets go inside PULPIT, between its I and T, giving PULPI-ES-T.
explanation.definitionFit: Pulpy is used of lurid, cheap fiction, so the superlative describes the most lurid, sensationalist material.

clue.text: Some fish guts on the counter ... pass the bucket

indicators.note: only some of the letters of the following words are taken, a run lying across them
counter means opposite in direction, so the run of letters is read the other way

blocks.note: the run straddling the end of fish and the start of guts

explanation.surface: Fish innards left on the kitchen counter make someone ask for a sick bucket.
explanation.walkthrough: The counter looks like a kitchen worktop, but it is the signal to read backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Asking for the bucket is a jokey way of voicing disgust, which the interjection expresses.

clue.text: Fool comes up with wise quotation

indicators.note: in a down clue rising upward means the word is read from the bottom, so backwards

blocks.note: a sap is a gullible fool
sage means wise

explanation.surface: A fool surprisingly produces a wise saying.
explanation.definitionFit: A passage is an extract from a text, the kind of excerpt that is quoted.

clue.text: Perfect bits of lovemaking requiring no tips

indicators.note: a thing without its tips has lost both its end letters

blocks.note: individual episodes of lovemaking, taken as two words

explanation.surface: A cheeky line about flawless lovemaking that needs no advice.
explanation.walkthrough: Tips sounds like advice, but it means the end letters of the phrase, both of which go.
explanation.definitionFit: Exact and perfect both mean precise and accurate in every detail, as in a perfect copy.

clue.text: Subtitle translated from French?

annotation.answer: TWENTY THOUSAND LEAGUES UNDER THE SEA

blocks.note: surface reading: the subtitles under a film, rendered from French dialogue
setter's reading: the title of a book about a submarine, translated from a French novel by Jules Verne

explanation.surface: Talk of reading the English subtitles on a French film.
explanation.walkthrough: Sub is read as submarine: Verne's novel about Captain Nemo's Nautilus is a sub title, and English readers know it only in translation.
explanation.definitionFit: Jules Verne wrote the novel in French as Vingt mille lieues sous les mers; the English name is a translation.

clue.text: Novel description of Methuselah, plus six of his characters

annotation.answer: THE OLD MAN AND THE SEA

blocks.note: Methuselah, who lived 969 years in Genesis, is the archetypal old man
plus means and
six of the ten letters of the name Methuselah, rearranged

explanation.surface: The setter, Methuselah, describing himself as a novel character.
explanation.walkthrough: Methuselah is also this puzzle's setter, so his characters are the letters of his name; T, H, E, S, E and A are drawn from it and put in order.
explanation.definitionFit: Ernest Hemingway's 1952 novella about the fisherman Santiago won him the Pulitzer Prize.

clue.text: Mistake is seized on by extremely tiresome bully

indicators.note: something seized is held in the grip of another, so these letters sit inside
the extremes of a word are its two outermost letters

blocks.note: the first and last letters of tiresome
a mistake is an error
taken as written

explanation.surface: A tedious bully pounces on someone's mistake.
explanation.definitionFit: To bully someone and to terrorise them both mean to intimidate them with threats or fear.

clue.text: A lot of ground covered by chauffeur as I abscond

indicators.note: what is covered by other words lies concealed within them

blocks.note: the run from the end of chauffeur to the first letter of abscond

explanation.surface: A runaway passenger confesses to fleeing a chauffeur who has driven a long way.
explanation.walkthrough: A lot of ground looks like distance travelled, but it is the definition: a vast landmass.
explanation.definitionFit: The combined continent of Europe and Asia is the largest landmass on Earth, a great deal of territory.

clue.text: Refined men chose eel spread

indicators.note: refined material has been processed and reworked, so these letters are recast

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Posh gentlemen opted to spread eel on their toast.
explanation.definitionFit: Lemon cheese is another name for lemon curd, a sweet preserve put on bread or toast.

clue.text: See 6
Every so often, rare medusa's shocking couple catching waves

indicators.note: something done every so often happens at intervals, so only alternate letters count
a shocking state is one of upheaval, so the letters are thrown into a new order

blocks.note: the first and third letters of rare
taken as written

explanation.surface: A rare jellyfish delivers a shock to a pair caught in the waves.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's stands for is, joining medusa to its anagram signal. The waves the couple catch are sound waves.
explanation.definitionFit: Each ear has a membrane that vibrates when sound waves strike it, so the pair of them pick up sound.

clue.text: Character back to fight insect superhero?

indicators.note: the back of a word is its end, so only its final letter is used

blocks.note: mu is a letter of the Greek alphabet, a character
the final letter of fight
an ant is an insect

explanation.surface: A comic-book character returns to battle an insect-themed superhero.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark marks the definition as an example: the X-Men are superheroes who are mutants.
explanation.definitionFit: In Marvel comics many superheroes, notably the X-Men, owe their powers to being genetic mutants.

clue.text: See 5
See 5
Sort of reaction produced by commercial poetry

blocks.note: a commercial is an advertisement, an ad
poetry is verse

explanation.surface: A rhyming advertisement provokes some kind of response.
explanation.definitionFit: An adverse reaction is a harmful or unwanted one, especially to a drug, so the adjective names a kind of reaction.

clue.text: Was private flogged raw after exposing lies?

indicators.note: exposing something strips its covering, so the outer letters go and the middle stays

blocks.note: to flog is slang for to sell
lies without its outer letters
red raw: raw skin is red

explanation.surface: A private soldier was flogged raw after his lies came out.
explanation.walkthrough: After places the red after the exposed lies. Flogged here means sold, not whipped.
explanation.definitionFit: A private is the lowest army rank, so to serve as one is to have soldiered.

clue.text: Shipwrecked boy discovered orang and hyena evacuated with another predator

indicators.note: dis-covered means with its cover removed, so the outer letters go
something evacuated has been emptied, so only its outer letters are left

blocks.note: Pi Patel is the shipwrecked boy of Yann Martel's novel Life of Pi
orang without its outer letters
hyena emptied of its middle letters

explanation.surface: A castaway boy shares a lifeboat with an orangutan, a hyena and one more predator.
explanation.walkthrough: In Life of Pi the boy's lifeboat holds an orangutan, a hyena and a tiger, so another predator fits the scene.
explanation.definitionFit: The piranha is a sharp-toothed South American fish that hunts other animals, so it is a predator.

clue.text: Spot clergyman getting unsolicited feedback from Cockney

indicators.note: a Cockney Londoner traditionally drops the H at the start of a word

blocks.note: Fr is the abbreviation for Father, a priest
a heckle is an interruption shouted at a speaker

explanation.surface: A priest gets heckled in East London.
explanation.walkthrough: Cockney is the working-class dialect of London's East End.
explanation.definitionFit: A freckle is a small brownish spot on the skin.

clue.text: Unequal readings of caesium and uranium give you pause

indicators.note: reading only part of each word, and different-sized parts, means taking opening letters of uneven length

blocks.note: the first four letters of caesium
the first three letters of uranium

explanation.surface: A lab note that mismatched measurements of two elements give a scientist pause.
explanation.walkthrough: Unequal is what tells you to take four letters of one element and three of the other.
explanation.definitionFit: A caesura is a break or pause in the middle of a line of verse.

clue.text: See 5
Blokes shortly get Scrooge half-cut with Bob

indicators.note: cut short, a word loses its final letter
half of the name is cut away, leaving its second half

blocks.note: taken as written
Ebenezer is the first name of Dickens's miser Scrooge
a bob was a shilling, abbreviated s

explanation.surface: Men get Scrooge drunk with Bob Cratchit's help.
explanation.walkthrough: Half-cut is British slang for tipsy, and Bob suggests Scrooge's clerk Bob Cratchit; here a bob is the old British shilling, written s.
explanation.definitionFit: Geezer is British slang for a man or fellow, as is bloke.

clue.text: Fancy aesthete binning a certain Lawrence novel

indicators.note: binning something throws it away, so those letters are removed
fancy means elaborate or fanciful, so the remaining letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
T. E. Lawrence, Lawrence of Arabia, known by his initials

explanation.surface: A fancy aesthete discards a novel by D. H. Lawrence.
explanation.walkthrough: A Lawrence novel suggests D. H.; the Lawrence meant is T. E., and the novel is a separate definition.
explanation.definitionFit: John Banville's novel of that name won the Booker Prize in 2005.

clue.text: Embarrassed sleuth breaks into exasperated expression

indicators.note: a burglar who breaks into a house ends up inside it

blocks.note: an exclamation of exasperation
a PI is a private investigator

explanation.surface: A red-faced detective interrupts someone's irritated outburst.
explanation.definitionFit: Sheepish describes the awkward, shamefaced look of someone embarrassed.

clue.text: Murdoch publication seethes with a hate that's out of order

indicators.note: letters out of order are no longer in their proper sequence

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A hostile reader fumes at a Rupert Murdoch newspaper's unacceptable conduct.
explanation.walkthrough: Murdoch suggests Rupert, the press baron; the author meant is Iris Murdoch.
explanation.definitionFit: Iris Murdoch's novel of that title won the Booker Prize in 1978.

clue.text: Spud sampler doesn't want seconds

indicators.note: what is not wanted is left out of the word

blocks.note: a taster samples food
s is the abbreviation for seconds

explanation.surface: A food sampler declines second helpings of potato.
explanation.walkthrough: Seconds looks like extra helpings, but it is the unit, abbreviated.
explanation.definitionFit: Tater and spud are both informal words for a potato.

clue.text: Landowners like stealing Irish resources, ultimately

indicators.note: a thief who steals something takes it in, so it ends up held inside
ultimately points to the very end, so only the final letter is used

blocks.note: the suffix -esque means like, in the style of
Ir is an abbreviation for Irish
the final letter of resources

explanation.surface: Absentee landlords plundering Ireland's wealth.
explanation.walkthrough: Like has to be read as the suffix, as in Kafkaesque.
explanation.definitionFit: An esquire was historically a member of the landed gentry ranking just below a knight.

clue.text: See 23
For example, Ovid's number one

blocks.note: e.g. abbreviates exempli gratia, for example
the first letter of Ovid

explanation.surface: A question about what came first in the Roman poet Ovid's work.
explanation.walkthrough: Ego is Latin for I, the word Ovid used for himself, so number one doubles as first letter and oneself.
explanation.definitionFit: Looking after number one means looking after oneself, the self that ego names.

clue.text: See 6
Graze from sabre unsheathed when principal spins around

indicators.note: a blade drawn from its sheath has its covering removed, so the outer letters go
something that spins around turns to face the other way, so it is read backwards

blocks.note: sabre without its outer letters
as means when, as in 'as I left'
the principal one is number one, No. 1

explanation.surface: A duellist suffers a cut when the chief swordsman wheels round.
explanation.definitionFit: An abrasion is a scrape on the skin, the injury left when something grazes it.
